practices-2-158-running-between-al-safa-.title: Running Between the Hills of al-Safa and al-Marwah in Pilgrimage
practices-2-158-running-between-al-safa-.note: Surah 2:158 reassures believers that there is no blame in pacing between al-Safa and al-Marwah, incorporating a pre-Islamic Arabian pilgrimage rite in which tribes ran between the two hills for the idols Manat, Isaf, and Na'ilah.

discussion.view: Muslim tradition holds that running between al-Safa and al-Marwah originated with Hagar's search for water for Ishmael, and that pre-Islamic Arabs later placed pagan idols on the two hills before Islam restored the Abrahamic rite.
discussion.reply: In Sahih al-Bukhari 1643, 4496, and Sahih Muslim 1277, Companions including Anas ibn Malik and the Ansar describe pacing between al-Safa and al-Marwah as a pre-Islamic custom performed for the idol Manat or the coastal idols Isaf and Na'ilah. Those reports record that early converts hesitated to perform the circuit because they recognized it as a pre-Islamic polytheistic ceremony.

practices-2-158-running-between-al-safa-.quranEn: Surely al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God. Whoever performs pilgrimage to the House or performs visitation – (there is) no blame on him if he goes around both of them. And whoever does good voluntarily – surely God is thankful, knowing.
quranHighlights: Surely al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God
(there is) no blame on him if he goes around both of them

sources.en: But in fact, this divine inspiration was revealed concerning the Ansar who used to assume Ihram for worshipping an idol called "Manat" which they used to worship at a place called Al-Mushallal before they embraced Islam, and whoever assumed Ihram (for the idol), would consider it not right to perform Tawaf between Safa and Marwa. When they embraced Islam, they asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) regarding it, saying, "O Allah's Apostle! We used to refrain from Tawaf between Safa and Marwa." So Allah revealed: 'Verily; (the mountains) As-Safa and Al-Marwa are among the symbols of Allah.' " Aisha added, "Surely, Allah's Apostle set the tradition of Tawaf between Safa and Marwa, so nobody is allowed to omit the Tawaf between them."

practices-2-187-white-thread-from-black-.title: Discerning the White Thread from the Black Thread at Dawn in Fasting
practices-2-187-white-thread-from-black-.note: Surah 2:187 permits eating, drinking, and marital relations on fast nights until 'a white thread may be discerned from a black thread at the dawn,' matching the dawn thread test in Mishnah Berakhot 1:2 and Berakhot 9b and fast abstinence in Mishnah Yoma 8:1.

discussion.view: Classical commentators explain the white and black threads as a divine metaphor for the streak of daybreak separating from the darkness of night, which some Companions initially took as literal cords until the words 'at the dawn' clarified the rule.
discussion.reply: In Mishnah Berakhot 1:2 (~AD 200) and Talmud Berakhot 9b (~AD 500), the dawn threshold is defined by looking at literal dyed and white wool threads on the ritual fringes (tzitzit) commanded in Numbers 15:38. Because Islamic law lacks the Torah fringe garment that generated the optical wool-thread test, the rabbinic legal rule had to be reinterpreted in Medina as a metaphor for the horizon.

practices-2-187-white-thread-from-black-.quranEn: It is permitted to you on the night of the fast to have sexual relations with your wives. They are a covering for you, and you are a covering for them. God knows that you have been betraying yourselves (in this regard), and has turned to you (in forgiveness) and pardoned you. So now have relations with them, and seek what God has prescribed for you. And eat and drink, until a white thread may be discerned from a black thread at the dawn. Then keep the fast completely until night, and do not have relations with them while you are devoted to the mosques. Those are the limits (set by) God, so do not go near them. In this way God makes clear His signs to the people, so that they may guard (themselves).
quranHighlights: permitted to you on the night of the fast to have sexual relations with your wives
eat and drink, until a white thread may be discerned from a black thread at the dawn

practices-2-142-145-fixed-qiblah-prayer-.title: Fixed Geographical Direction of Prayer (Qiblah) and Shift from Jerusalem
practices-2-142-145-fixed-qiblah-prayer-.note: Surah 2:142–145 transitions the community from praying toward Jerusalem to facing the Meccan sanctuary, building on the biblical and rabbinic law of facing Jerusalem in Daniel 6:10, Mishnah Berakhot 4:5, and Talmud Berakhot 30a.

discussion.view: Traditional commentators state that praying toward Jerusalem was a temporary divine command in Medina to test who would follow the Prophet, before God restored the primordial Abrahamic sanctuary in Mecca as the permanent direction of prayer.
discussion.reply: Fixing daily prayer toward Jerusalem and its Temple is anchored in 1 Kings 8:44–48, Daniel 6:10, Mishnah Berakhot 4:5 (~AD 200), and Talmud Berakhot 30a (~AD 500). Adopting the Jerusalem prayer orientation upon arriving among Medinan Jewish tribes, and shifting to the Meccan sanctuary roughly sixteen months later after Jewish rejection, tracks the historical realignment of the Medinan polity.

And We established the direction (of prayer) which you were (facing) toward only so that We might know the one who would follow the messenger from the one who would turn back on his heels. Surely it was hard indeed, except for those whom God guided. But God was not one to let your belief go to waste. Surely God is indeed kind (and) compassionate with the people. [144] We do see you turning your face about in the sky, and We shall indeed turn you in a direction which you will be pleased with. Turn your face in the direction of the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces in its direction. Surely those who have been given the Book know indeed that it is the truth from their Lord. God is not oblivious of what they do. [145] Yet even if you bring every sign to those who have been given the Book, they will not follow your direction. You are not a follower of their direction, nor are they followers of each other’s direction. If indeed you follow their (vain) desires, after the knowledge which has come to you, surely then you will indeed be among the evildoers.

stories-2-249-251-talut-river-drinking-t.title: Talut (Saul) Testing Troops at the River Like Gideon Before Slaying Goliath
stories-2-249-251-talut-river-drinking-t.note: Surah 2:249–251 attributes to King Talut (Saul) the river-drinking test of Gideon's army from Judges 7:4–7—separating those who drink freely from those who scoop water by hand—immediately before David slays Jalut (Goliath) as in 1 Samuel 17:48–51.

discussion.view: Muslim commentators explain this passage either as a separate unrecorded test conducted by King Saul on the march to face Goliath or as an intentional prophetic parallel between two Israelite campaigns.
discussion.reply: In the Hebrew Bible, the river test separating three hundred men who scoop water with their hands from the rest of the army belongs to the judge Gideon fighting the Midianites (Judges 7:4–7). King Saul's campaign against the Philistines and David's slaying of Goliath occur generations later in 1 Samuel 17, where no river-drinking test takes place.

stories-2-249-251-talut-river-drinking-t.quranEn: [249] When Ṭālūt set out with his forces, he said, ‘Surely God is going to test you by means of a river. Whoever drinks from it is not on my side, but whoever does not taste it is surely on my side, except for whoever scoops (it) up with his hand.’ But they (all) drank from it, except for a few. So when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, ‘We have no strength today against Jālūt and his forces.’ But those who thought that they would meet God said, ‘How many a small cohort has overcome a large cohort by the permission of God? God is with the patient.’ [250] So when they went forth to (battle) Jālūt and his forces, they said, ‘Our Lord, pour out on us patience, and make firm our feet, and help us against the people who are disbelievers.’ [251] And they routed them by the permission of God, and David killed Jālūt, and God gave him the kingdom and the wisdom, and taught him about whatever He pleased. If God had not repelled some of the people by means of others, the earth would indeed have been corrupted. But God is full of favor to the worlds.

stories-2-67-73-red-heifer-and-unsolved-.title: Combining the Unblemished Red Cow and the Heifer for an Unsolved Murder
stories-2-67-73-red-heifer-and-unsolved-.note: Surah 2:67–73 merges two distinct Torah statutes into one narrative: the unblemished, unworked cow of Numbers 19:2–3 and the unworked heifer slaughtered for an unknown homicide in Deuteronomy 21:1–4, adding that striking the corpse revives the victim.

discussion.view: Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir recount an Israelite inheritance murder in which God commanded the sacrifice of a specific golden-yellow cow so that striking the slain man with its bone or flesh would bring him back to name his killer.
discussion.reply: In the Pentateuch, Numbers 19:2–9 prescribes burning an unblemished, unworked red cow to produce purification ashes for corpse-contamination, while Deuteronomy 21:1–9 prescribes breaking the neck of an unworked heifer in a valley to absolve a town of an unsolved murder. Neither statute involves striking a corpse with the cow to resurrect the victim.

practices-2-199-pouring-forth-from-arafa.title: Pouring Forth from 'Arafat and Reforming the Pre-Islamic Quraysh Hums Rite
practices-2-199-pouring-forth-from-arafa.note: Surah 2:199 commands Quraysh to 'press on from where the people press on' at 'Arafat, reforming the pre-Islamic Hums privilege whereby Quraysh halted at Muzdalifah while other Arabs stood at 'Arafat.

discussion.view: Classical exegetes state that Abraham originally stood at 'Arafat, and that the Quraysh later innovated the Hums privilege of remaining inside the sanctuary border at Muzdalifah until Surah 2:199 restored Abraham's station.
discussion.reply: Hadith reports in Sahih al-Bukhari 4520 and Tafsir al-Tabari on 2:199 document that both the station at 'Arafat and the rushing procession (ifadah) through Muzdalifah were established pre-Islamic Arabian pilgrimage ceremonies. Surah 2:199 unified the two pre-Islamic tribal itineraries by requiring the Meccan Hums to join the wider Arab pilgrim assembly at 'Arafat.

practices-2-228-three-month-waiting-peri.title: Three-Period Post-Divorce Waiting Term ('Iddah) to Ascertain Pregnancy
practices-2-228-three-month-waiting-peri.note: Surah 2:228 requires divorced women to wait three periods before remarrying so as not to conceal what is in their wombs, matching the three-month waiting period and paternity rationale in Mishnah Yevamot 4:10.

discussion.view: Muslim jurists view the three-cycle waiting period ('iddah) as a revealed legal measure ensuring paternity certainty and giving estranged spouses a structured window for reconciliation.
discussion.reply: The Mosaic Torah contains no three-month post-divorce waiting rule. The mandatory three-month waiting period before a divorced or widowed woman may remarry—along with its explicit rationale of ascertaining pregnancy and paternity—was codified centuries earlier in Mishnah Yevamot 4:10 (~AD 200) and Talmud Bavli Yevamot 42b (~AD 500).

practices-2-228-three-month-waiting-peri.quranEn: (Let) the divorced women wait by themselves for three periods. It is not permitted to them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day. Women rightfully have the same privilege (as is exercised) over them, but men have a rank above them. God is mighty, wise.

sources.title: Mishnah Yevamot 4:10
sources.en: A yevama may neither perform ḥalitza nor enter into levirate marriage until she has waited three months from the time of her husband’s death. And similarly, all other women may not be betrothed and may not marry until they have waited three months since their previous marriage ended. This waiting period is necessary so that, should a woman give birth shortly after remarrying, it will be obvious who the father of the child is. This applies both to virgins and non-virgins, both to divorcées and widows, and both to women who were married to their previous husbands and women who were only betrothed. All of these women must wait three months before remarrying even though for some of them the reason for doing so does not apply.

practices-2-173-fourfold-dietary-ban-and.title: Fourfold Dietary Prohibition and the Life-Saving Necessity Exemption
practices-2-173-fourfold-dietary-ban-and.note: Surah 2:173 forbids carrion, blood, swine flesh, and idol-dedicated meat while exempting those forced by life-saving necessity, combining Acts 15:28–29, Leviticus 11:7–8, and Talmud Yoma 82a (pikuach nefesh).

discussion.view: Islamic theology regards the prohibition of carrion, blood, pork, and idol-consecrated meat—paired with mercy for one forced by starvation—as the original prophetic dietary law perfected in the Quran.
discussion.reply: Whereas the Mosaic Torah lists dozens of forbidden land, sea, and winged creatures in Leviticus 11, the compact fourfold list of idol-sacrificed meat, blood, carrion/strangled animals, and pork reproduces the Apostolic Decree of Acts 15:28–29 as observed by Late Antique Eastern Christians, combined with the rabbinic life-saving necessity exemption (pikuach nefesh) codified in Talmud Yoma 82a.

practices-2-173-fourfold-dietary-ban-and.quranEn: He has only forbidden to you: the dead (animal), and the blood, and swine’s flesh, and what has been dedicated to (a god) other than God. practices-2-189-entering-houses-from-bac.title: Pre-Islamic Pilgrimage Taboo of Entering Houses from Their Backs
practices-2-189-entering-houses-from-bac.note: Surah 2:189 declares that 'it is not piety to come to your houses from their backs, but come to your houses by their doors,' abolishing the pre-Islamic Arabian taboo in which pilgrims in Ihram climbed into their homes from behind.

discussion.view: Commentators explain that Surah 2:189 abolished a pre-Islamic superstition added by Arabian tribes to the Abrahamic pilgrimage, teaching that true piety lies in reverence toward God rather than ritual taboos.
discussion.reply: Sahih al-Bukhari 1803 and 4512 and Tafsir al-Tabari on 2:189 record that the Ansar and non-Hums Arabs observed the state of ritual consecration (ihram) before Islam by refusing to pass under door lintels, whereas Qurayshi Hums exempted themselves. The verse presupposes and directly legislates within this local Hijazi tribal distinction between Hums and non-Hums pilgrims.

practices-2-189-entering-houses-from-bac.quranEn: They ask you about the new moons. Say: ‘They are appointed times for the people, and for the pilgrimage.’ It is not piety to come to (your) houses from their backs, but (true) piety (belongs to) the one who guards (himself). Come to (your) houses by their doors, and guard (yourselves) against God, so that you may prosper.

practices-2-233-twenty-four-month-nursin.title: The Fixed Two-Full-Year (Twenty-Four-Month) Breastfeeding Term
practices-2-233-twenty-four-month-nursin.note: Surah 2:233 stipulates that mothers shall nurse their children for two full years (24 months) while fathers provide maintenance or hire a wet nurse, matching the exact 24-month nursing term in Talmud Ketubot 60a and 59b.

discussion.view: Islamic family law treats the two-year nursing term and the father's duty to compensate a divorced mother or wet nurse as divine legislation revealed to protect infant welfare and maternal rights.
discussion.reply: Neither the Hebrew Bible nor the New Testament legislates a fixed two-year nursing period. Talmud Bavli Ketubot 60a (~AD 500) establishes the exact twenty-four-month statutory nursing term, and Ketubot 59b pairs it with the legal rule requiring a divorced father to pay a wet-nurse wage if the infant recognizes its mother.

practices-2-233-twenty-four-month-nursin.quranEn: Mothers shall nurse their children for two full years, for those who wish to complete the nursing (period). (It is an obligation) on the father for him (to supply) their provision and their clothing rightfully. No one is to be burdened beyond their capacity. A mother is not to suffer on account of her child, nor a father on account of his child. The (father’s) heir has a similar (obligation) to that. If the two of them wish, by mutual consent and consultation, to wean (the child earlier), (there is) no blame on (either of) them. And if you wish to seek nursing for your children, (there is) no blame on you, provided you pay what you have rightfully promised. Guard (yourselves) against God, and know that God sees what you do.

However, if he ceased, i.e., was weaned, after twenty-four months and then resumed nursing, he is like one who nurses from a non-kosher animal.

discussion.view: Classical commentators explain that God informed the angels of Adam's appointment on earth and demonstrated Adam's divinely taught knowledge by having him name every creature before them.

stories-2-259-sleeper-for-hundred-years-.title: The Man Sleeping a Hundred Years Beside His Donkey and Unspoiled Food
stories-2-259-sleeper-for-hundred-years-.note: Surah 2:259 recounts a traveler questioning how a ruined city will be restored, sleeping for a hundred years beside his food and his donkey while supposing a single day has passed, matching the Talmudic narrative of Honi ha-Me'aggel in Taanit 23a.

discussion.view: Commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify the traveler variously as Ezra (`Uzayr`), Jeremiah, or Khidr passing by Jerusalem after its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar.
discussion.reply: In Talmud Bavli Taanit 23a, Honi ha-Me'aggel questions how the 70-year Babylonian exile of Jerusalem relates to Psalm 126:1, falls asleep beside his donkey and food for 70 years, and wakes to learn that generations have passed. Surah 2:259 fuses this Talmudic sleeper-and-donkey narrative with Ezekiel's vision of dry bones clothed with sinews and flesh in Ezekiel 37:7–8.

He said, ‘How will God give this (town) life after its death?’ So God caused him to die for a hundred years, (and) then raised him up. He said, ‘How long have you remained (dead)?’ He said, ‘I have remained (dead) for a day or part of a day.’ He said, ‘No! You have remained (dead) for a hundred years. Look at your food and drink, it has not spoiled, and look at your donkey – and (this happened) so that We might make you a sign to the people – and look at the bones, how We raise them up, (and) then clothe them with flesh.’ So when it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that God is powerful over everything.’

stories-2-102-solomon-demons-and-harut-m.title: Demons in Solomon's Reign and the Two Angels Harut and Marut in Babylon
stories-2-102-solomon-demons-and-harut-m.note: Surah 2:102 links demons in Solomon's kingdom teaching magic with two angels in Babylon named Harut and Marut, combining 1 Enoch 7–8 on fallen angels teaching sorcery with Talmud Gittin 68a on Solomon's male and female demons.

discussion.view: Classical exegetes explain that Surah 2:102 exonerates Solomon of practicing sorcery while affirming that God sent two angels, Harut and Marut, to Babylon as a test regarding magic.
discussion.reply: The narrative combines three Near Eastern traditions: Talmudic legends in Gittin 68a giving Solomon authority over demons, the Second Temple Book of Watchers (1 Enoch 7–8) where angels descend and teach humans charms and root-cuttings, and the paired Zoroastrian archangels (`Amesha Spentas`) Haurvatat/Horvadad and Ameretat/Amerodad, whose Middle Persian names correspond philologically to Harut and Marut.

They taught the people magic, and what had been sent down to the two angels (in) Babylon, Hārūt and Mārūt. Neither of them taught anyone, unless they both (first) said, ‘We are only a temptation, so do not disbelieve.’ And they learned from both of them how to separate a husband from his wife. Yet they did not harm anyone in this way, except by the permission of God. What they learned (only) harmed them and did not benefit them. Certainly they knew that whoever buys it has no share in the Hereafter. Evil indeed is what they have sold themselves for, if (only) they knew.

stories-2-65-66-sabbath-breakers-transfo.title: Transgressors Transformed into Apes as Divine Punishment in Sanhedrin 109a
stories-2-65-66-sabbath-breakers-transfo.note: Surah 2:65–66 recounts God punishing Israelite Sabbath violators by commanding them, 'Become apes, skulking away,' paralleling the Talmudic punishment in Sanhedrin 109a where rebels against God are transformed into apes.

discussion.view: Traditional commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that an Israelite coastal community violated the Sabbath by trapping fish on Saturday and was physically transformed into apes for three days before perishing.
discussion.reply: In the Torah (Exodus 31:14–15; Numbers 15:32–36), the penalty for Sabbath violation is capital execution, and no biblical passage records humans being transformed into apes. Physical transformation of rebels against God into apes (`kofim`) is a rabbinic aggadic punishment recorded by Rabbi Yirmeya bar Elazar in Talmud Bavli Sanhedrin 109a.

phrases-2-286-do-not-lay-on-us-a-burden-.note: Surah 2:286 states 'God does not burden any person beyond his capacity' and prays 'do not lay on us a burden such as You laid on those before us,' matching Acts 15:10 ('a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear') and 1 Cor 10:13.

discussion.view: Muslim tradition regards the closing verses of Surah al-Baqarah as a direct heavenly gift relieving the Muslim community of the strict legal covenants imposed on earlier nations.

phrases-2-93-sinai-we-hear-and-disobey.title: Sinai Covenant Inversion: 'We Hear and Disobey' vs. 'We Will Hear, and Do'

discussion.view: Classical commentators explain that while the Israelites spoke obedience with their tongues at Sinai, their rebellious hearts inwardly replied 'We hear and disobey.'
discussion.reply: In Deuteronomy 5:27, Israel pledges at Sinai 'we will hear, and do' (Hebrew shamaʿnu we-ʿasinu), a phrase celebrated in Talmud Bavli Shabbat 88a; because the Hebrew verb ʿasinu ('we will do') sounds like the Arabic verb ʿaṣaynā ('we disobey'), Surah 2:93 turns the Torah's vow of obedience into a declaration of defiance ('We hear and disobey').

stories-2-63-mount-sinai-raised-overhead.title: Surah 2 Covenant Reminder of Mount Sinai Raised Above Israel
stories-2-63-mount-sinai-raised-overhead.note: Surah 2:63 addresses the Children of Israel directly, recalling how God took their covenant while raising the mountain physically above them (rafa'na fawqakumu l-tura), reproducing the midrashic reading of Exodus 19:17 in Talmud Shabbat 88a.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Israelites hesitated to accept the heavy obligations of the Torah, angels uprooted Mount Sinai and held it suspended over their heads until they bowed in acceptance.
discussion.reply: While 7:171 uses nataqna ('We shook the mountain above them as a canopy'), 2:63 states the motif in the second person (rafa'na fawqakumu l-tura) during Israel's covenant indictment. In Exodus 19:17 the Israelites stand at the foot (be-tachtit) of Mount Sinai; Talmud Bavli Shabbat 88a and Avodah Zarah 2b read be-tachtit literally ('beneath') to teach that God overturned the mountain above them like a tub.

practices-2-238-239-guarding-the-middle-.title: Guarding the Middle Prayer (Salat al-Wusta) and Praying Riding in Fear
practices-2-238-239-guarding-the-middle-.note: Surah 2:238–239 commands guarding the daily prayers, especially 'the middle prayer,' and praying on foot or riding when in fear, matching the afternoon prayer vigilance in Talmud Berakhot 6b and the danger and riding prayer rules in Mishnah Berakhot 4:4–5.

discussion.view: Hadith collections and commentators identify 'the middle prayer' primarily with the afternoon prayer ('Asr) and cite Surah 2:239 as the scriptural basis for the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) on foot or horseback.
discussion.reply: Talmud Bavli Berakhot 6b (~AD 500) singles out the afternoon prayer (Minhah) for special vigilance because of midday commercial distractions, while Mishnah Berakhot 4:4–5 (~AD 200) explicitly legislates how a traveler walking in a place of danger or riding an animal performs a shortened prayer without dismounting.

practices-2-238-239-guarding-the-middle-.quranEn: [238] Watch over the prayers, and the middle prayer. And stand before God obedient. [239] If you fear (danger), (pray) on foot or (while) riding. But when you are secure, remember God, since He has taught you what you did not know.

stories-2-34-angels-prostrate-to-adam-ib.title: Surah 2 Account of the Angels Bowing to Adam After the Naming Scene
stories-2-34-angels-prostrate-to-adam-ib.note: Immediately after Adam recites the names of all things before the angels in 2:31–33, Surah 2:34 narrates God commanding the angels to prostrate before Adam while Iblis refuses in arrogance, matching Vita Adae et Evae 13–15 and the Cave of Treasures.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that in 2:34 God commanded the angels to bow to Adam as a greeting of honor after Adam demonstrated superior knowledge by naming the creatures, whereas Iblis refused out of envy and pride.
discussion.reply: Unlike 7:12, 15:33, and 38:76, which give Iblis's fire-versus-clay argument, 2:34 places the command to prostrate immediately after Adam's naming of the creatures (2:31–33) and attributes Iblis's refusal simply to arrogance (istakbara). This sequence directly parallels the Syriac Cave of Treasures, where Adam names all creatures on his throne before the angels bow the knee and the rebellious archangel refuses.

practices-2-183-185-prescribed-fasting-a.title: Prescribed Fasting with Make-Up Days for Sickness or Travel
practices-2-183-185-prescribed-fasting-a.note: Surah 2:183–185 prescribes fasting 'as it was prescribed for those before you' and allows the sick or travelers to make up missed days later, combining Numbers 9:10–11, Mishnah Yoma 8:5, and pre-Islamic 'Ashura fasting in Bukhari 4504.

discussion.view: Muslim exegetes state that God prescribed fasting for earlier prophetic communities and transitioned the Muslim community from the earlier fast of 'Ashura to the month of Ramadan with merciful exemptions for illness and travel.
discussion.reply: Surah 2:183 explicitly appeals to the precedent of earlier communities ('as it was prescribed for those who were before you'). Its rule allowing a traveler to postpone the fast to an equal count of later days mirrors the Second Passover travel-postponement law of Numbers 9:10–11, combined with the illness exemption of Mishnah Yoma 8:5 and the pre-Islamic/Jewish 'Ashura fast in Sahih al-Bukhari 4504.

practices-2-183-185-prescribed-fasting-a.quranEn: [183] You who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those who were before you, so that you may guard (yourselves). [184] (Fast for) a number of days. Whoever of you is sick or on a journey, (let him fast) a certain number of other days. And for those who can afford it, (there is) a ransom: feeding a poor person. Whoever does good voluntarily – it is better for him. But to fast is better for you, if (only) you knew. [185] The month of Ramaḍān, in which the Qur’ān was sent down as a guidance for the people, and as clear signs of the guidance and the Deliverance: so whoever of you is present during the month, let him fast in it, but whoever of you is sick or on a journey, (let him fast) a certain number of other days. God wishes to make it easy for you, and does not wish any hardship for you. And (He wishes) that you should fulfill the number (of days), and that you should magnify God for having guided you, and that you should be thankful.
